nature-gov-197.title: Conservation refugees
nature-gov-197.text: In Guinea, 663,000 people have been displaced from protected areas. Liberia claims over 120,000 conservation refugees, and Senegal has 65,000 displaced. A conservation refugee is a person, usually Indigenous, pushed from their homeland when a park or reserve is created. Many were already marginalized. They end up on the edges of towns with few opportunities and rarely have legal recourse. The idea behind it is old. John Muir's view that wilderness should be emptied of inhabitants became US policy with the 1964 Wilderness Act. The anthropologist Darrell Posey disagreed, arguing that landscapes that look natural may have been shaped by Indigenous peoples.

nature-gov-219.title: Locally unwanted land uses
nature-gov-219.text: Nobody wants a landfill, power plant or prison next door. Planners call such a project a locally unwanted land use: a facility a community opposes because of the harms it expects. Those harms include health hazards, ugliness, lower home values and sometimes higher utility bills. Such facilities tend to land in poor, minority or politically weak places that cannot fight them off. They then keep wealthier buyers away, trapping low-income residents in cheap housing near dumps and highways. Of more than 1,000 US Superfund toxic sites, 25% lie on or near Native American reservations.

nature-gov-224.title: Sacrifice zones
nature-gov-224.text: Louisiana's "Cancer Alley" runs 85 miles along the Mississippi, lined with over 200 petrochemical plants. Its population is disproportionately Black and low-income. It is a sacrifice zone: an area permanently damaged by heavy environmental change or economic neglect, often through land uses no one else would accept. A 2022 UN report found that millions of people live in pollution sacrifice zones, mostly around heavy industry and mining, with marginalized groups hit hardest. The phrase has roots in a 1973 US National Academy of Sciences report on strip-mined coal lands in the American West, which spoke of a "national sacrifice area." Sacrifice zones have a mirror image, "abundance zones." Damage in some places sustains privilege elsewhere. Naomi Klein argued in 2014 that an economy run on fuels that release poisons when extracted has always needed sacrifice zones.

nature-gov-225.title: Thinking seven generations ahead
nature-gov-225.text: Live and work for the good of the seventh generation to come. That principle is believed to come from the Great Law of the Haudenosaunee, which judges decisions by their effects seven generations ahead. The often-quoted line does not actually appear in written versions of the Haudenosaunee constitution. That text instead urges leaders to consider future generations. Some green economists advise judging a project's impacts from the viewpoint of the seventh generation.

nature-gov-208.title: Ethnoecology: how cultures read their environment
nature-gov-208.text: According to the WHO, almost 80% of the world's people rely on traditional plant-based remedies as a main source of treatment. Ethnoecology studies how different groups of people understand the ecosystems around them and their own place in them. Harold Conklin coined the term in his 1954 dissertation on how the Hanunoo culture relates to plants. To learn how cultures classify their surroundings, it borrows methods from linguistics and anthropology. It treats humans as part of ecosystems. People can act as a keystone species, shaping soil formation, seed dispersal and biodiversity.

nature-gov-194.title: Atmospheric colonization
nature-gov-194.text: Countries of the Global North hold 19% of the world's people but account for 92% of accumulated greenhouse gas emissions. The Global South accounts for 8%. Atmospheric colonization is the idea that rich countries have taken over most of the sky's capacity to absorb greenhouse gases, leaving poorer countries to bear the results. Countries such as Ecuador emit relatively little carbon dioxide but have far fewer resources to cope with local climate impacts.

nature-gov-195.title: Climate apartheid: when only the rich escape
nature-gov-195.text: When Superstorm Sandy hit in 2012, most of New York lost power. Goldman Sachs's headquarters had its own generator and sandbags. UN Special Rapporteur Philip Alston cited that contrast in June 2019. He warned of climate apartheid, a world where only the rich can escape climate change. He said it could undermine human rights, democracy and the rule of law.

nature-gov-203.title: Ecological distribution conflicts
nature-gov-203.text: When a factory pollutes a river, the market usually puts no price on the harm, so the people downstream go uncompensated. In 1995, Joan Martínez-Alier and Martin O'Connor coined a term for such fights: ecological distribution conflicts. These are clashes over unfair access to natural resources and unequal pollution burdens. Mainstream economics treats such harms as externalities, costs to outsiders that could be priced. Ecological economists and political ecologists reject the idea that money can measure them. Movements may ask for money when weak, but argue from values money cannot measure when strong.

nature-gov-206.title: The environmentalism of the poor
nature-gov-206.text: Chipko villagers hugging trees in India, Indigenous groups resisting Brazilian agribusiness, Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement: all are examples of the environmentalism of the poor. These are movements that arise when poor people fight powerful state or private interests threatening their livelihood, health, sovereignty and culture. Mainstream environmentalism centers on conservation and efficiency. This kind puts social justice first. Martinez-Alier describes it as poor people's struggles in conflicts where an activity's harms fall unevenly and unjustly. Peruvian historian Alberto Flores Galindo suggested the term in 1988. In 1997 Martinez-Alier and Ramachandra Guha contrasted it with the "full-belly environmentalism" of the global North. Women often lead, because fetching water and growing crops bring them into direct contact with nature. The risks are mortal. Leaders such as Berta Cáceres and Chico Mendes were assassinated. International justice networks now help local defenders seek support against large corporations.

nature-gov-228.title: Who pays for green policy?
nature-gov-228.text: A carbon tax that keeps its revenue hits the poorest households hardest. That is because it is regressive: its burden falls, as a share of income, the richer people are. The distributional effects of an environmental policy describe how its costs and benefits fall on different groups, and whether it widens or narrows injustice. They are one of the standard tests for judging policy, alongside efficiency and cost-effectiveness. The pattern varies. One study found carbon pricing is on average progressive in countries with incomes below USD 15,000 a head, but tends to be regressive in richer ones. A 2019 study found energy efficiency standards more regressive than energy taxes. Because carbon pricing leans regressive, economists say poor people should be compensated. Not all agree on the premise: Gilbert Metcalf disputed that a US carbon tax would be regressive. Global estimates of climate damage usually leave these effects out.

nature-gov-183.title: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
nature-gov-183.text: In 2007 the United Nations adopted a declaration setting out the collective rights of Indigenous peoples. Those rights include self-determination and the protection of cultures, identities, languages, ceremonies and access to resources. The declaration does not define Indigenous peoples. It affirms instead their right to decide their own identity. It is the clearest statement of free, prior and informed consent in international development. It also offers benchmark standards on Indigenous land rights.

nature-gov-205.title: Environmental personhood: when a river becomes a person
nature-gov-205.text: In 2017, New Zealand declared the Whanganui River a legal person. It is represented by two guardians, one from the Māori iwi and one from the Crown. Environmental personhood is a legal idea that gives natural features, such as rivers or forests, the status of a legal person. That brings rights and liabilities. A river cannot go to court, so a guardian acts for it. And a legal person cannot be owned. Christopher D. Stone first proposed the idea in the 1970s, in an article titled "Should trees have standing?" An Indian state court gave the Ganges and Yamuna rivers similar status in March 2017. Skeptics noted that words alone would not stop the pollution. In 2022 Spain made the Mar Menor lagoon the first ecosystem in Europe with its own rights. Supporters say people can then sue for nature without showing harm to humans. Critics ask who is liable if a river is sued over a flood. Even some environmentalists reject it.

nature-gov-221.title: Rawls's three kinds of procedural justice
nature-gov-221.text: In A Theory of Justice, John Rawls split procedural justice into three forms. Perfect procedural justice has an independent standard of a fair result and a procedure that guarantees reaching it. Imperfect procedural justice has the standard but no procedure that guarantees the fair result. Pure procedural justice has no standard of a just result apart from the procedure itself.

nature-gov-174.title: Environmental reparations
nature-gov-174.text: Environmental reparations are payments or investments made to people judged to be harmed by industry. Recipients might be people living near industry, disaster victims or climate refugees. The forms vary widely: direct payouts, funds to clean waste sites, air monitors in low-income neighborhoods, or public transport.

nature-gov-188.title: Climate refugees and the gap in the law
nature-gov-188.text: Asian and African mega-deltas and small islands face high risks of floods and storms, and possibly displacement on a large scale. People forced to move by climate change fall into a legal gap, because international law does not yet cover such migration. The International Organization for Migration defines environmental migrants as people obliged or choosing to leave home because environmental change harms their lives. Climate migration is one of the most disputed effects of climate change. How many people will move, and who counts as a climate refugee, remain undefined in law.

nature-gov-216.title: Aboriginal title: land rights that outlive conquest
nature-gov-216.text: In 1971, Meriam people in Australia began a case that would overturn a legal fiction. In the Mabo case, the High Court recognized native ownership and rejected terra nullius, the doctrine that the land had belonged to no one. Aboriginal title is the common-law rule that Indigenous peoples' customary land rights survive after a settler state takes sovereignty. It is called native title in Australia, customary title in New Zealand and original Indian title in the US. American law went the other way first. In Johnson v. McIntosh (1823), the doctrine of discovery was used to rule that Native Americans had only rights of occupancy.

nature-gov-207.title: Three kinds of environmentalism
nature-gov-207.text: Joan Martinez-Alier divides environmentalism into three currents. The cult of the wilderness, tied to older conservation campaigns, tries to keep economic activity away from nature, mainly through reserves. It has at times expelled poor and Indigenous people to create them. The gospel of eco-efficiency accepts growth but wants growth that uses fewer resources and makes less waste. Critics say physical laws limit efficiency gains, and that rich economies cut material use only by outsourcing heavy production to poorer countries. The third current is environmental justice, the environmentalism of the poor.

nature-gov-189.title: Ancestral domain: more than a land title
nature-gov-189.text: Many Indigenous peoples would rather be called custodians of their lands than owners. Tradable private land was often a colonial import. Ancestral domain, a term used especially in the Asia-Pacific region, means the lands, territories and resources of Indigenous peoples. Unlike a land title, "domain" covers spiritual and cultural ties, not just ownership that can be sold. The Philippines' Indigenous People's Rights Act of 1997 defines it to include lands, inland waters, coasts and natural resources. International law shifted too. The ILO's 1957 Convention No. 107 assumed Indigenous peoples would be absorbed into wider society. Convention No. 169 replaced it in 1989.

nature-gov-211.title: Feminist political ecology
nature-gov-211.text: Environmental policies that seem gender-neutral can overlook what women know about managing resources. Feminist political ecology studies how gender shapes people's access to, control over and knowledge of natural resources. It treats three areas as gendered: knowledge, environmental rights and grassroots activism. It explains differences in experience through social ideas about gender, not biology. A key founding text is the 1996 book Feminist Political Ecology by Dianne Rocheleau and colleagues.

nature-gov-223.title: Writing the rights of nature into law
nature-gov-223.text: Ecuador's 2008 constitution gives nature, or Pachamama, the right to exist and to renew its vital cycles. Any person may demand those rights be respected. Rights of nature law writes this idea into constitutions, statutes, treaties, local laws and court rulings. It treats ecosystems and species as having inherent rights, much like human rights. As of 2022 such laws existed in 39 countries, and initiatives grew from 409 in June 2021 to 495 in May 2024. In 2019, Bangladesh's High Court declared the Turag River, and by extension all the country's rivers, living entities with legal rights.

nature-gov-229.title: Gender and the environment
nature-gov-229.text: Women do 80% of food production in sub-Saharan Africa, 60% in Asia and 50% in Latin America. Men generally own the land. The study of gender and environment examines how relations between women, men and nature shape resource use, divide responsibilities and affect well-being. Interest grew from Ester Boserup's 1960s book Woman's Role in Economic Development, and policymakers paid more attention from the 1980s. Improving women's access to farm resources could raise their yields by 20–30% and total farm output in poor countries by 2.5–4%. Some feminist economists argue that the focus on growth sustains gender and environmental injustice, and propose shorter, shared work.

nature-gov-181.title: ILO Convention 169
nature-gov-181.text: In 1989 the International Labour Organization adopted a treaty on Indigenous and tribal peoples. ILO Convention 169 aims to end discrimination against them and give them a role in decisions, built on participation and consultation. The duty to consult falls on the state, not on companies. Its aim is agreement or consent to a proposed development.

nature-gov-182.title: Consent protocols written by Indigenous peoples
nature-gov-182.text: Since the early 2000s, Indigenous peoples have written their own rules for how consent processes must run. These are FPIC protocols. The first were tied to specific sectors. The second were bio-cultural protocols linked to the Biodiversity Convention's rules on access to genes. The third, mostly from Latin America, are autonomous protocols.

nature-gov-005.title: Poverty: lacking the basics
nature-gov-005.text: As of 2019, measured in dollars adjusted for local prices, 85% of people lived on less than $30 a day. Two-thirds lived on less than $10, and 10% on less than $1.90. Poverty is lacking the money and essentials needed for a basic standard of living. Absolute poverty compares income with what basic needs cost, such as food, clothing and shelter. Relative poverty compares living standards with others in the same time and place. The famous "dollar a day" line, introduced in 1990, became US$1.90 a day in 2015. It is measured at purchasing power parity, meaning what money buys locally, rather than at exchange rates. Poverty and nature are closely tied. Poor people are more exposed to the environmental effects of industry, climate change, disasters and extreme weather. Economic pressure on poor communities often plays a part in deforestation and biodiversity loss. Growth does not always help: the poorest citizens of middle-income countries often fail to gain enough of the new wealth to escape. Sustainable Development Goal 1, "No Poverty," adopted in 2015, sums up the international framework for ending it.

nature-gov-006.title: Does poverty damage nature, or protect it?
nature-gov-006.text: Developing countries suffer 99% of the casualties attributable to climate change. Yet about 92% of accumulated greenhouse gas emissions are attributed to the Global North. That lopsided split of burdens and benefits gave rise to the global movements for environmental justice and climate justice. The link between poverty and environmental damage runs both ways. The poor tend to suffer most when natural resources are exploited and ecosystems degrade. A 2016 UN report claimed that by 2030 climate change could push an additional 122 million people into extreme poverty. Does poverty also cause degradation? Here the experts split. The Brundtland Report concluded that it does. The environmentalism-of-the-poor view holds the opposite: the global poor may be the most important force for sustainability. Conservation itself can burden the poor too. Fortress conservation has evicted Indigenous people, and green colonialism grabs land in the name of environmentalism.

nature-gov-007.title: Degraded land and deprivation: a vicious circle
nature-gov-007.text: In 2025, 47 million stunted children under five lived where stunting overlaps with large harvest losses from land degradation. Southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa are where degraded land and deep poverty coincide. Land degradation and deprivation reinforce each other. Damaged land brings lower yields, less food, more exposure to floods and droughts, lost homes and economic trouble. It can also lose its natural ability to store and filter water, causing shortages. Most of sub-Saharan Africa shows fairly low losses from degradation. That is not because its soils are healthier. Poor access to fertilizer, machinery, credit and markets holds yields down even more. Of the world's 570 million farms, 85% are under 2 hectares and work just 9% of farmland, which limits what farmers can do. Degradation sharpens competition for land. All but 3 conflicts inside African states since the 1990s are linked to it. It can also drive people to migrate.

nature-gov-001.title: The cycle of poverty
nature-gov-001.text: Children born into poverty depend on their guardians and are too young to work their own way out. That makes them the most vulnerable part of the cycle of poverty, also called a poverty trap. In this situation, poverty seems to pass down, and later generations cannot escape it. Self-reinforcing forces keep it going unless someone from outside steps in. Lack of money, education and social connections all hold families in place. Applied to whole developing countries, the idea is called a development trap. The cycle has an environmental edge. People living in degraded ecosystems may want sustainable options but cannot afford to let land and resources regenerate. The cycle also makes climate harms worse. Conditional cash transfers, payments tied to steps such as schooling or health checks, aim to help families now and break the cycle for the next generation.

nature-gov-003.title: Sustainable livelihoods
nature-gov-003.text: Poverty is not only a lack of money. The sustainable livelihoods idea widens the view to include vulnerability and social exclusion. It asks how people, especially vulnerable groups, can support themselves in ways that last and can bounce back from shocks. The Brundtland Commission introduced the idea. The 1992 UN Conference on Environment and Development made sustainable livelihoods a broad goal for ending poverty. The approach favors development centered on people and shaped by their participation, linking environmental and economic concerns. The 17 Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015 for 2030, are one example. The COVID-19 pandemic set back goals such as SDG 1, No Poverty.

nature-gov-009.title: Cheap water that misses the poor
nature-gov-009.text: Poor families without a piped connection often buy water from vendors at about 5 to 16 times the metered price. Meanwhile, subsidies that make piped water cheap flow mainly to households already connected, typically richer urban ones outside informal settlements. With heavy subsidies, water prices in developing countries cover on average only 30% of supply costs. Utilities then have little reason to maintain or extend their networks. Leaks lose enough water for 200 million people a year, and many poor homes stay unconnected. Subsidizing new connections has shown more promise.

nature-gov-008.title: Energy poverty and development
nature-gov-008.text: Businesses, schools, clinics and homes all run on energy, so lacking it holds development back. Poor energy access is linked to infant mortality, illiteracy and shorter lives, and can push people to move to cities. Energy use and economic growth have historically risen together, though it is unclear which drives the other. By the early 2000s, rich countries were growing without a matching rise in energy use. In developing countries the two stayed tightly linked. Energy-poor households often burn wood and dung, which release black carbon, a health hazard, when they burn incompletely.

nature-gov-002.title: Why whole countries stay poor
nature-gov-002.text: Some countries stay stuck in poverty as a whole, held back by lack of credit, degraded land, corruption, disease, war and poor infrastructure. Extreme environmental degradation is one cause, because it cuts what farmland can produce. Jeffrey Sachs argues that the extreme poor lack six kinds of capital, natural capital among them. When population grows faster than savings, capital per person can shrink each generation. Sachs argues that large, lasting foreign aid can lift households above subsistence. He wants public money spent on health, education, infrastructure and natural capital, such as conserving ecosystems, leaving business investment to private firms.

nature-gov-004.title: Five kinds of capital for a livelihood
nature-gov-004.text: The United Nations Development Programme sizes up how people make a living by the five kinds of capital they can draw on. Human capital is skills and health. Social capital is relationships. Natural capital is land, water and other resources. Physical capital is tools and infrastructure, and financial capital is money. How much people can reach of each shapes how the UNDP designs its projects. The framework also asks how people use these assets to cope with shocks. The UK's Department for International Development and the charity CARE use similar frameworks instead of sector-by-sector approaches.

reviews.justice-rights-and-indigenous-knowledge: The chapter's central fact is a mismatch: those who did least to cause environmental harm often bear the most of it, from Warren County's landfill and Cancer Alley to Pakistan's floods. Indigenous peoples stand at the sharp end, as their lands are mined for export, their knowledge patented, and their homes cleared for parks that make conservation refugees. Yet when their hold on land is secure, through recognized title or territories of life, forests fare better than under fortress conservation. Movements have answered with new tools: consent before development, benefit-sharing for genes, rights to a healthy environment, and even legal personhood for rivers. Each rests on two kinds of fairness, a fair share of costs and benefits and a fair say in how decisions are made.
reviews.poverty-development-and-the-environment: Poverty and environmental damage feed each other. Degraded land cuts harvests and income, and families caught in a poverty trap cannot afford to let land and resources recover. The Brundtland Report blamed poverty for degradation, while others see the poor as a leading force for sustainability, and both sides agree the poor suffer first. Even well-meant help can miss them, as water subsidies flow to richer connected homes. Approaches built on livelihoods and the five kinds of capital, natural capital among them, try to help people support themselves in ways that last.

openers.poverty-development-and-the-environment: Most of the world's people live on less than $10 a day, and the poorest depend most directly on land, water and forests. When that land degrades, food and income fall, and families can sink into a cycle of poverty that later generations cannot escape. Whole countries can be stuck the same way, held back by degraded land, disease, war and poor infrastructure. This short chapter looks at how poverty and environmental damage reinforce each other, and at ways of thinking about livelihoods that last.
